questions.question: An HR Q&A bot gives answers that are accurate but full of jargon. The developer adds this line to the prompt: "Explain the answer so that a new intern with no HR background can easily follow it." Which prompt framework element does this line mainly supply?

options.text: Role
options.explanation: Role sets the identity the model assumes (for example, "You are a senior developer"). This line describes who will read the answer, not who the model is.

options.text: Audience
options.explanation: This is the answer. Audience names the target readers of the output, like "Explain this to a 5-year-old", which adjusts complexity and tone to suit them.

options.text: Context
options.explanation: Context gives background about the task, such as operational processes or scenarios. It does not say who the output is written for.

options.text: Output Format
options.explanation: Output Format covers the output's format, type and allowed enumerated values. Who the answer is for is a separate element.

questions.takeaway: Audience controls how complex and what tone the output has by naming who will read it.

questions.question: A team is reviewing how it uses the basic prompt framework elements. Which statements describe those elements accurately?

options.text: Role identifies the group of end users who will read the model's response.
options.explanation: This describes Audience. Role is the persona the model takes on, which shapes its voice and writing style.

options.text: Context gives background such as operational processes or task scenarios, which sets the scope the model should consider.
options.explanation: This is accurate. Context sets the scope of the discussion by describing the task's background.

options.text: Sample gives concrete input-output examples for the model to follow, also called few-shot prompting.
options.explanation: This is accurate. Samples show the model the pattern and format it should copy.

options.text: Objective is where retrieved reference documents are placed so the model can ground its answer.
options.explanation: Objective states what task the model must complete. Retrieved material is background information and goes in the context part of the prompt.

options.text: Output Format can also list content that must not appear in the output, and examples can make this clearer.
options.explanation: This is accurate. The framework says Output Format can say what to exclude and can be backed up with examples.

questions.takeaway: Each framework element has its own job: objective (task), context (background), role (persona), audience (readers), sample (examples), output format (shape and exclusions).

questions.question: A developer wants the company FAQ bot to include official links whenever it recommends software tools. As a quick fix, they append "Please make sure to include the official website or download link for the tools in your response." to every user question. What is the main weakness of this approach?

options.text: The added sentence makes every question longer than the model's context window, so long answers get cut off.
options.explanation: One extra sentence is a tiny amount of text. The problem shown in the notebook is with relevance, not length.

options.text: The model ignores instructions that come after the user's question, so it will never add the links.
options.explanation: For the tools question, the model did follow the instruction and gave links. The instruction is followed, not ignored.

options.text: The model only follows instructions placed in the system role, so text added to the user message has no effect.
options.explanation: The appended instruction clearly changed the output. Where the instruction sits is not the problem here.

options.text: The same instruction is added to unrelated questions, such as annual leave, which produces awkward and wordy answers, and someone would have to decide by hand which instruction suits each query.
options.explanation: This is the answer. This one-size-fits-all patch is fragile. It does not adapt to the type of question and cannot scale in a real application.

questions.takeaway: Hard-coded instructions added to every query are fragile. Build the context systematically so it fits each situation.

sources.heading: 2. Optimizing Prompts to Improve Response Quality

questions.question: In the default LlamaIndex RAG prompt template, the text includes the placeholders {context_str} and {query_str}. At query time, what replaces {context_str}?

options.text: Relevant information retrieved from the vector database
options.explanation: This is the answer. context_str is filled with the retrieved content, and query_str is replaced with the user's actual question.

options.text: The user's question, after it has been rewritten by the model
options.explanation: The user's question goes into query_str, not context_str.

options.text: The system role description, such as "You are the company's customer service assistant"
options.explanation: Role text is written into the template string by the developer. It is not a placeholder filled during retrieval.

options.text: The model's earlier answers from the conversation history
options.explanation: The template shown only fills in retrieved context and the current query. It does not insert chat history.

questions.takeaway: Template placeholders separate fixed instructions from changing inputs: context_str holds retrieved knowledge, query_str holds the user's question.

questions.question: An enterprise is deploying a RAG-based FAQ bot. Why should the developers build a custom prompt template instead of asking employees to write good prompts themselves or relying only on the default template?

options.text: End users cannot realistically be expected to write effective prompts from scratch. A template lets developers insert user input into predefined placeholders.
options.explanation: This is a valid reason. The notebook says templates exist because end users should not have to engineer prompts.

options.text: Templates keep every final prompt consistent, which leads to more reliable and standardized responses.
options.explanation: This is a valid reason. Consistency is the main benefit of templates that the notebook describes.

options.text: A template guarantees factually correct answers even when the retrieved context is wrong or missing.
options.explanation: A template shapes how the model responds. It cannot fix bad or missing knowledge. Grounding still depends on what is retrieved.

options.text: The default template is general-purpose. A custom template can set the tone, add constraints, or define an exact output format for the scenario.
options.explanation: This is a valid reason. The notebook customizes the template so the output matches specific requirements.

options.text: A well-written template removes the need for retrieval because the instructions alone give the model the company's private knowledge.
options.explanation: Instructions do not add knowledge. RAG is still needed to fill context_str with company information.

questions.takeaway: Prompt templates apply framework principles consistently and let you tailor tone, constraints and format to the scenario.

questions.question: A legal-review assistant processes contracts that use many square-bracket references such as [Clause 4.2] and [Annex B]. The developer needs to separate the contract text from the instructions in the prompt. Which approach best follows delimiter best practice?

options.text: Wrap the contract in square brackets, because the model is already used to seeing brackets in this content.
options.explanation: Symbols that appear often in the content make poor delimiters. The model could not tell the real boundary from the in-text references.

options.text: Leave out delimiters and paste the contract right after the instruction, because delimiters only matter for very short inputs.
options.explanation: Delimiters help the model focus and avoid misreading the prompt. They matter even more when long input sits next to instructions.

options.text: Wrap the contract in XML-like tags such as <contract>...</contract>, which do not appear in the text.
options.explanation: This is the answer. Pick a delimiter that does not occur in the content. XML-like tags separate content cleanly from instructions.

options.text: Use square brackets for both the instructions and the contract so the whole prompt has one consistent style.
options.explanation: Using the same symbol for instructions and content makes it harder, not easier, to tell them apart.

questions.takeaway: Pick delimiters that never appear in your content so section boundaries are clear.

sources.heading: 4.1 Clearly express requirements and use delimiters

questions.question: A prompt uses ### Instruction ###, === Original Text === and <text>...</text> to organize a copywriting task. Which benefits does this use of delimiters provide?

options.text: It helps the model focus on the specific goal of each part of the prompt.
options.explanation: This is a benefit. The notebook says delimiters help LLMs focus on specific goals.

options.text: It reduces the chance that the model misreads which part is instruction and which part is material.
options.explanation: This is a benefit. Delimiters help avoid ambiguous readings and unnecessary processing.

options.text: It isolates the original content so the model knows exactly which text to rewrite or expand.
options.explanation: This is a benefit. In the training-camp example, <text>...</text> wraps the original copy that needs polishing.

options.text: It makes the RAG engine skip retrieval for the delimited part of the prompt.
options.explanation: Delimiters only structure the prompt text for the model. They do not change how retrieval works.

options.text: It makes the prompt more readable and better structured, for people and for the model.
options.explanation: This is a benefit. The notebook says delimiters improve readability and how well the model understands the prompt.

questions.takeaway: Delimiters structure a prompt so the model can tell instructions, inputs and output requirements apart.

sources.heading: 4.1 Clearly express requirements and use delimiters

questions.question: Two RAG bots use the same retrieved context and the same question, "What is Qwen-VL?". One template starts with "You are a senior large language model algorithm engineer" and the other with "You are an elementary school teacher." The first answer is technical and talks about application areas. The second uses simple analogies and emojis for children. What does this comparison show?

options.text: The role changes which documents are retrieved, so each bot answers from different knowledge.
options.explanation: Both bots share the same context_str. The difference comes from the persona in the template, not from retrieval.

options.text: Personas make answers less accurate, so production templates should leave out roles.
options.explanation: Both answers describe Qwen-VL correctly. The notebook presents role definition as a technique to use, not to avoid.

options.text: A role only changes how long the answer is. Tone and structure come only from output format instructions.
options.explanation: The two outputs differ a lot in tone, vocabulary and structure, not just length. Role shapes all of these.

options.text: Defining a role, and with it the implied audience, changes the tone, depth and structure of the output while the facts stay the same.
options.explanation: This is the answer. Role and audience let developers tailor the style of the content for the scenario.

questions.takeaway: Role and audience shape the tone, depth and structure of an answer without changing the facts underneath.

questions.question: A content-review pipeline sends articles to an LLM to check spelling and grammar. A downstream service parses the result automatically to set revision priority. Which prompt design best supports this integration?

options.text: State that the output must be JSON only, with no markdown or code blocks, and define each field: "label" (0 if an error is found, 1 if not), "reason", and "correct".
options.explanation: This is the answer. Stating the format, the field names and the enumerated values gives consistent output that a program can parse.

options.text: Ask for a clear, friendly paragraph about the errors, and have the downstream service pull out the details with keyword matching.
options.explanation: Free-form text is hard to parse reliably. The notebook asks for structured output so it is easy to integrate.

options.text: Ask for JSON, but let the model decide which fields to include so it can adjust to each article.
options.explanation: If the model chooses the fields, the schema changes from call to call and the downstream parser breaks. Fields and values should be spelled out.

options.text: Ask for JSON wrapped in a markdown code block, because the code fence makes the JSON easier to parse.
options.explanation: The notebook's prompt says not to include markdown or code blocks, because extra wrapping gets in the way of direct parsing.

questions.takeaway: For machine-readable output, specify the exact format, the fields, the allowed values and what to leave out.

questions.question: A prompt already asks for Markdown tutorials in a step-by-step format, but the generated "Handmade Keychain Making Tutorial" is too long and its structure varies. The developer adds a short bookmark-making tutorial inside <example>...</example> tags, and the next output, "Making Handmade Greeting Cards", closely follows that structure. Which conclusions are supported?

options.text: Format instructions can get the format right but may not keep style and structure consistent. Examples fill that gap.
options.explanation: This is supported. The notebook adds few-shot examples so the output is consistent in style and structure as well as correctly formatted.

options.text: Wrapping the example in <example> tags keeps the reference material separate from the instructions and the user's topic.
options.explanation: This is supported. This combines few-shot prompting with delimiters so the model knows which part is the template to copy.

options.text: The example has to be on the same topic as the user's request, or the model will not follow its structure.
options.explanation: The example (a bookmark) and the request (greeting cards) are on different topics. The model copies the structure, not the subject.

options.text: Few-shot prompting acts like a "reference book" the model can imitate.
options.explanation: This is supported. The notebook uses this same comparison for few-shot prompting.

options.text: Few-shot prompting works by updating the model's weights with the examples before it generates text.
options.explanation: Few-shot examples are only part of the prompt context. No training or weight update takes place.

questions.takeaway: Add a few examples next to format rules when you need the output's style and structure to stay consistent.

questions.question: A prompt gives this data: 5 business trips at an average of 1,600 USD each for transport and accommodation, and teaching materials bought for 10,000 USD that are expected to last 4 years. It asks for the total travel expenses for the year including amortized materials, and ends with "Provide only the total travel expenses directly, without any other information." The model returns a wrong number. Which revision follows the technique from the notebook and leads to the correct total?

options.text: Keep the instruction to give only the final number, but add a stronger role, such as "You are a certified accountant", so the model is more careful.
options.explanation: The failure comes from forcing an instant answer to a multi-step calculation. A role alone does not give the model room to reason.

options.text: Replace the output requirement with "Please derive step by step to calculate the total travel expenses", so the model works out 5 x 1,600 = 8,000 plus 10,000 / 4 = 2,500, giving 10,500 USD.
options.explanation: This is the answer. Chain-of-thought prompting has the model show its intermediate steps, which improves accuracy on logic and math tasks.

options.text: Add a few-shot example of a correctly formatted single-number answer so the model copies the format.
options.explanation: Few-shot examples fix format and style. The problem here is the reasoning, not how the answer looks.

options.text: Move the background data after the question so the model reads the task before the numbers.
options.explanation: Changing the order does not fix the real issue, which is asking for a direct answer with no intermediate reasoning.

questions.takeaway: For multi-step logic or math, give the model time to think by asking it to reason step by step.

questions.question: A team moves a complex analysis task from a general-purpose model to a reasoning model with thinking mode turned on. The old prompt contains "Think step by step and explain your reasoning before answering." What is the recommended change?

options.text: Keep the phrase, because reasoning models only start their thinking process when they see it.
options.explanation: Reasoning models think deeply on their own. The phrase is not what turns on their thinking process.

options.text: Make the chain-of-thought instructions stronger by giving a detailed reasoning procedure for every task.
options.explanation: Strict reasoning templates are only useful when a fixed approach is truly required, which is rare. Otherwise they can limit the model.

options.text: Usually remove the step-by-step instruction, because reasoning models already reason deeply and such prompting may limit their performance.
options.explanation: This is the answer. The notebook advises against chain-of-thought prompting with reasoning models unless a fixed reasoning path is needed.

options.text: Replace it with few-shot examples of full reasoning chains, because reasoning models cannot reason without demonstrations.
options.explanation: Reasoning models produce their own thinking process. Examples are for clarifying abstract requirements, not for making the model reason.

questions.takeaway: Do not add chain-of-thought instructions for reasoning models. They already think, and extra guidance can hold them back.

sources.heading: 5.2 Prompt Techniques Suitable for Reasoning Models

questions.question: An architect is deciding which LLM tasks should go to a reasoning model instead of a general-purpose model. For which tasks does the notebook recommend a reasoning model?

options.text: An ambiguous request with very little information, where the team cannot give the model clear guidance
options.explanation: Recommended. The notebook lists ambiguous tasks with little information as a use case for reasoning models.

options.text: Extracting fields from short, well-structured forms in a high-volume pipeline with a tight latency budget
options.explanation: A clearly defined task that is sensitive to time and cost suits a general-purpose model, which is faster and cheaper.

options.text: Searching a large amount of unstructured data to find the most relevant facts and the links or differences between them
options.explanation: Recommended. This is the "needle in a haystack" case the notebook gives for reasoning models.

options.text: Reviewing, debugging and improving a large codebase
options.explanation: Recommended. Debugging and improving a lot of code is listed as a reasoning-model task.

options.text: Converting already-cleaned records from CSV to JSON on a cost-sensitive budget
options.explanation: Format conversion is a simple, well-defined task. The notebook assigns this kind of work to general-purpose models.

questions.takeaway: Use reasoning models for ambiguous, complex or high-precision work. Use general-purpose models for clear, cost-sensitive tasks.

questions.question: A company wants an agent-style assistant that handles complex multi-step requests with high-quality results, while keeping latency and operating costs under control. Which design best follows the notebook's guidance?

options.text: Use a reasoning model as the planner or analyst that breaks down complex tasks, and give the simpler subtasks to general-purpose models or tools to carry out.
options.explanation: This is the answer. Mixing the two model types gives deep thinking where it is needed and fast, cheap execution elsewhere.

options.text: Send every step, including simple extraction and formatting, to a reasoning model, because reasoning models are always better.
options.explanation: The notebook says reasoning models are not always better. They are slower and cost more, which is wasted on simple steps.

options.text: Use only a general-purpose model for everything, and add "think step by step" to each prompt to get the same planning quality.
options.explanation: Chain-of-thought helps general models, but the notebook recommends reasoning models for complex planning and meta-tasks.

options.text: Use a general-purpose model for planning and a reasoning model for routine execution, because planning should be fast.
options.explanation: This reverses the recommended split. Planning and decision-making benefit most from the reasoning model's deep thinking.

questions.takeaway: Combine models: reasoning models plan and analyze, general-purpose models execute the smaller subtasks cheaply.

sources.heading: Technique 4: Let Reasoning Models Be Your "Prompt Coach"

questions.question: Which statements correctly compare reasoning models with general-purpose models, based on the comparison in the notebook?

options.text: General-purpose models usually output a complete derivation, while reasoning models keep their answers short and direct.
options.explanation: This is reversed. Reasoning models show complete derivations, and general-purpose models give concise, direct answers.

options.text: Reasoning models produce an extra thinking process and can go back and adjust their approach when they find a contradiction at some step.
options.explanation: This is correct. The thinking process works like scratch paper and cuts down on off-the-cuff mistakes.

options.text: Reasoning models answer faster on complex tasks because they skip single-step generation.
options.explanation: Reasoning models answer more slowly on complex tasks because they work through multiple steps.

options.text: Reasoning models are trained with a focus on math solutions, code logic and scientific reasoning data, while general-purpose models cover encyclopedias, literature and conversations.
options.explanation: This is correct. It matches the training-data row in the notebook's comparison table.

questions.takeaway: Reasoning models trade speed for visible, self-correcting multi-step reasoning. General models are faster and more concise.

questions.question: A developer thinks the onboarding bot's answer about company benefits is accurate but bland and disorganized, and wants to use meta prompting to improve the prompt. Which meta prompt is most likely to produce a useful optimized prompt?

options.text: "Make this prompt better." followed only by the initial prompt
options.explanation: Without the output and specific goals, the model does not know what is wrong or what "better" means. Results will be unpredictable.

options.text: The initial prompt and an instruction to answer the employee's question directly in a friendlier way
options.explanation: This asks the model to answer the employee instead of rewriting the prompt, so you get one better answer but no reusable prompt.

options.text: The generated output only, with a request to list its grammar mistakes
options.explanation: Proofreading the output is not the same as improving the prompt, and it ignores the real goals of tone and structure.

options.text: The initial prompt, the output it produced, specific requirements (a warm, welcoming tone, emoji bullet points, benefits grouped into categories such as "Health & Leave"), and a request to rewrite the prompt as a prompt engineering expert
options.explanation: This is the answer. Clearly stating the problem and the expectations lets the "AI coach" understand your intent and produce a targeted rewrite.

questions.takeaway: A good meta prompt gives the coach the current prompt, its output, the specific gaps, and a request to rewrite.

sources.heading: 4.6 Meta Prompting: Let the LLM Be Your Prompt Coach

questions.question: A team finds that giving the AI coach qualitative goals such as "friendlier" leads to unpredictable optimizations. They switch to a multi-round loop built around a high-quality reference answer. Which description of this loop is accurate?

options.text: The optimizer LLM compares the generated response with the reference answer and returns Pass or Fail, and the loop stops at the first Pass.
options.explanation: In this loop, the comparison is done by an evaluator (Critic) that writes a detailed gap report. A Pass/Fail AI Judge comes later as an upgrade.

options.text: A Critic LLM compares the generated response with the reference answer and writes a gap analysis report covering tone, structure, content and format. An optimizer LLM then rewrites the prompt using that report, the current prompt and the generated response. This repeats until the gap is minimal or the maximum number of iterations is reached.
options.explanation: This is the answer. This is the five-step reference-answer loop: set the reference, generate, analyze the gap, optimize, repeat.

options.text: The reference answer is pasted into the generation prompt as a few-shot example, so no evaluation step is needed.
options.explanation: The reference answer is the target for gap analysis, not an example for the generator to copy. The loop depends on a separate evaluation step.

options.text: The loop keeps running until the generated response matches the reference answer word for word.
options.explanation: The stopping condition is a minimal gap or a maximum number of iterations, not an exact text match.

questions.takeaway: Using a reference answer turns vague prompt tuning into measurable gap analysis between a Critic and an Optimizer.

sources.heading: Multi-Round Iteration: Introducing Reference Answers for Gap Analysis

questions.question: A team builds an "AI Judge" prompt that labels bot responses Pass or Fail, and refines it in the way the notebook describes. Which practices match that process?

options.text: Collect the misjudged cases from the evaluation set and give them to the optimizer, so the judge learns from data it will later be tested on.
options.explanation: The process uses wrong answers from the training set. The evaluation set is kept apart to detect overfitting.

options.text: Track accuracy on both the training set and the evaluation set in each round, so you can tell when the judge has only memorized the training samples.
options.explanation: This matches. If evaluation accuracy stalls or drops while training accuracy rises, that suggests overfitting.

options.text: If new wrong answers show ambiguous or contradictory labels in the samples, stop iterating and fix the labeled data first.
options.explanation: This matches. With poor-quality samples, the LLM may never manage to build a good judge.

options.text: Adopt the version of the judge prompt that performs best on the evaluation set as the final AI Judge.
options.explanation: This matches. The final judge is chosen by how well it performs on the evaluation set.

options.text: Treat the judge prompt as the "model" being trained and the labeled good/bad samples as the "dataset", for example split 7:3 into training and evaluation sets.
options.explanation: This matches. The notebook frames building the judge like training a machine learning classifier.

questions.takeaway: Build an AI Judge like a classifier: labeled data, train/eval split, learn from training errors, and choose the version by evaluation performance.

sources.heading: 4.7 Let the LLM Help You Build a Custom "AI Judge"

questions.question: In the improved workflow, a validated AI Judge returns Pass or Fail for each generated response. When the judge returns Fail, what does the optimizer receive so it can rewrite the generation prompt?

options.text: Only the failed response, so the optimizer can find and fix the problem sentences directly
options.explanation: Without the generation prompt, the optimizer has nothing to rewrite, and without the judge's rules it does not know the failure criteria.

options.text: The reference answer and a gap analysis report, the same as in the earlier qualitative loop
options.explanation: This workflow replaces the gap-analysis step with the AI Judge. The optimizer is given the judge's rules instead.

options.text: The current generation prompt, the failed response, and the AI Judge's prompt as a rulebook with clear failure criteria
options.explanation: This is the answer. Giving the optimizer the judge's rulebook lets it rewrite the prompt specifically so the next response passes.

options.text: The full labeled training set used to build the judge, so the optimizer can retrain the judge
options.explanation: The training set was used to build the judge. In this loop, the goal is to improve the generation prompt, not the judge.

questions.takeaway: Build the judge first, then improve the generator: a reliable Pass/Fail judge gives a clear stopping point and clear rules for fixes.

sources.heading: 4.7.4 Use the "AI Judge" to Guide Automated Optimization

questions.question: A developer wants to show objectively which of three prompt versions produces the best company-benefits introduction. They use an LLM as a "Grader". Which design choices match the notebook's approach?

options.text: Define each scoring dimension (for example welcoming_tone, structuring, visual_appeal, completeness) on a 1-5 scale, and describe what 1 and 5 mean for each.
options.explanation: This matches. Clear anchors for each dimension turn vague feelings into consistent, measurable scores.

options.text: Have the grader write a free-form critique, and have people turn it into numbers afterward.
options.explanation: The notebook has the grader return structured scores directly, so they can be compared and charted automatically.

options.text: Require the grader to return only JSON scores, and parse the output defensively with a fallback when it is not valid JSON.
options.explanation: This matches. The grader prompt asks for strict JSON, and the code extracts the JSON and uses default scores if parsing fails.

options.text: Use a single overall Pass/Fail result, because per-dimension scores are too noisy to compare across versions.
options.explanation: Pass/Fail is how the AI Judge decides when to stop. Comparing versions here relies on scores for each dimension.

questions.takeaway: Quantitative LLM grading needs explicit criteria, scales and structured output so you can compare prompt versions with evidence.
